text: What is the scope resolution operator in C++, and what is it used for?
expectedAnswerPoints: The :: operator accesses a name that lies outside the current scope, or that belongs to a particular class or namespace
It reaches a global variable when a local variable of the same name is shadowing it, written as ::x
It defines a member function outside the class body, as in void Student::show(), which keeps the class declaration readable
It qualifies a namespace member such as A::value, and accesses static members through the class itself, as in ClassName::count

It also resolves ambiguity under multiple inheritance, allowing obj.Base1::show() to state which inherited version is meant; Java has no equivalent operator and relies on the dot with package qualification

text: Does Java support multiple inheritance? Explain the reasoning behind the answer.
expectedAnswerPoints: Java does not allow a class to extend more than one class, but it does allow a class to implement any number of interfaces

The reason for the restriction is ambiguity: if two parent classes each supplied a different implementation of the same method, the compiler would have no basis for deciding which one the child inherits
That ambiguity is the diamond problem, and C++ takes the opposite route, permitting multiple inheritance and requiring explicit qualification or virtual inheritance to resolve it
Interfaces avoided the problem because classically they carried no implementation at all, so the implementing class was forced to provide exactly one version of each method itself

Java 8 default methods reintroduced the possibility of a conflict, and Java handles it by making the clash a compile-time error that the class must resolve explicitly using InterfaceName.super.method()

text: What is an interface in Java, and what can it contain?
expectedAnswerPoints: An interface is a contract specifying what a class must be able to do, without prescribing how it does it
Its methods are implicitly public and abstract, and its fields are implicitly public static final, which is to say constants
It cannot have constructors or instance state, which is why an interface can never be instantiated directly

Since Java 8 an interface may contain default methods with a body, which allows a new method to be added without breaking every existing implementer, and static methods belonging to the interface itself

Since Java 9 it may also contain private methods to share code between default methods; the enduring differences from an abstract class are that interfaces support multiple inheritance and hold no instance state

text: Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can you declare a pointer to an abstract class in C++?
expectedAnswerPoints: Yes, an abstract class can have a constructor, and usually should, because it has instance fields that need initialising as part of every derived object
That constructor is never used to create an abstract object directly: it runs as part of constructing a derived object, invoked by the derived class constructor
Neither language allows an abstract class to be instantiated: C++ refuses because at least one pure virtual function has no implementation, and Java rejects any use of new on an abstract type

You can absolutely declare a pointer or reference to an abstract class in C++, or a variable of an abstract type in Java, and that is precisely how polymorphism is used, holding a derived object through a base handle

Identifies the distinction being tested: declaring a handle of an abstract type is legal and routine, whereas creating an object of that type is not, and an abstract class should also declare a virtual destructor since it exists to be held polymorphically

text: What are the rules for method overriding in Java?
expectedAnswerPoints: Overriding means a subclass supplies its own implementation of a method already declared in its superclass
The method name and parameter list must match exactly; a different parameter list produces an overload in the subclass rather than an override
The return type must be identical or a covariant subtype, so an override is permitted to return a more specific type than the parent declared

The access modifier may not be more restrictive than the parent's, since anything callable through the parent type must remain callable, and a checked exception thrown may not be broader than the parent declared
Static, final and private methods cannot be overridden; overriding is resolved at run time from the actual object type, which is what makes it run-time or dynamic polymorphism

text: What does the final keyword do in Java, and how does it differ from finally and finalize?
expectedAnswerPoints: A final variable can be assigned only once and never reassigned, which is how constants are declared, usually together with static
A final method cannot be overridden by any subclass, which locks in behaviour the class author does not want changed
A final class cannot be extended at all, which is why String is declared final and cannot be subclassed
Applied to a reference, final makes the reference immutable rather than the object: a final List can still have elements added to it, only the variable cannot be pointed at something else
Distinguishes the similarly named terms: finally is a block that always runs after a try or catch, and finalize is the deprecated cleanup hook that ran before garbage collection

text: Can a static method be overridden in Java? Explain what actually happens.
expectedAnswerPoints: No: a static method belongs to the class rather than to any instance, so there is no object whose actual type could drive dynamic dispatch
Declaring a static method in a subclass with the same signature is method hiding rather than overriding, and the two are resolved by completely different rules
Which version runs is decided at compile time from the reference type, so a Parent-typed reference pointing at a Child object will call the Parent version
Instance methods behave the opposite way: in exactly the same situation the Child version runs, because dispatch uses the actual object type rather than the reference type
Because the two cases look identical in source but behave differently, calling a static method through an instance reference is misleading and should always be written as ClassName.method() instead

text: What does the super keyword do in Java?
expectedAnswerPoints: super refers to the immediate parent class from inside a subclass
super.method() calls the parent version of a method the subclass has overridden, which is how an override extends the parent behaviour rather than replacing it entirely
super.field accesses a parent field that a subclass field of the same name is hiding
super(...) calls a parent constructor, and where it is used it must be the very first statement in the subclass constructor

If neither an explicit super nor a this constructor call is written, the compiler inserts a no-argument super() automatically, which is why a parent lacking a no-argument constructor forces the child to call one explicitly
private: visible only inside the declaring class, and not even to its subclasses
default, also called package-private, which applies when no modifier is written at all: visible to any class in the same package but nowhere outside it
protected: visible throughout the package and additionally to subclasses in other packages
public: visible from everywhere

Notes the contrast with C++, which has only private, protected and public and no package concept, and gives the design guidance that fields should start private and visibility should be widened only when genuinely needed

text: What is upcasting and downcasting, and why is one safe and the other not?
expectedAnswerPoints: Upcasting converts a derived reference to a base reference and is always safe, so it happens implicitly with no cast written
It is what makes polymorphism usable in practice: a collection of Animal references can hold Dogs and Cats, and a virtual call still dispatches to the actual type
Upcasting narrows what is visible rather than what exists: only members declared in the base type can be called through the base reference, even though the object remains a complete derived object
Downcasting converts a base reference back to a derived one and is unsafe, because the object may not really be of that type, which is why it must be written explicitly

Guarding it: Java throws ClassCastException at run time so instanceof should be checked first, while C++ dynamic_cast returns nullptr for pointers or throws for references; a downcast that keeps appearing is usually a sign the design should have used a virtual method instead

text: What is constructor overloading, and what happens if a class defines no constructor at all?
expectedAnswerPoints: Constructor overloading provides several constructors differing in their parameter lists, so an object can be created with different amounts of information supplied
If a class declares no constructor whatsoever, the compiler supplies a default no-argument constructor that performs default initialisation
That implicit constructor disappears the moment any constructor is declared, so writing only a parameterised constructor makes the no-argument form a compile error
Constructors can delegate to one another to avoid duplicated initialisation code, using this(...) in Java or a delegating constructor in C++
Notes what a constructor cannot be: it has no return type, it is not inherited, and it cannot be virtual, although it can be overloaded

text: When should you prefer composition over inheritance?
expectedAnswerPoints: Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship, where the derived type genuinely is a kind of the base type; composition expresses has-a, where one object holds another as a member

Inheritance is the tighter coupling, because the subclass depends on its parent internals, so a change to the parent can break subclasses that were never touched, which is the fragile base class problem
Composition is more flexible, since the contained object can be swapped at run time and only its public interface is depended upon

Applies the substitution test: use inheritance only when a derived object can be used anywhere the base is expected without surprising the caller, so a Car should hold an Engine rather than extend one
States the standard design guidance to prefer composition by default, reserving inheritance for genuinely substitutable is-a relationships

text: What is the difference between aggregation and composition?
expectedAnswerPoints: Both are has-a relationships, and what separates them is ownership and lifetime
Aggregation is a weak has-a: the contained object can exist independently of the container, and destroying the container does not destroy it
Composition is a strong has-a: the lifetime of the contained object is bound to the container, so destroying the container destroys it as well

Gives examples that make the distinction concrete, such as a department aggregating professors who continue to exist if the department closes, versus a house composed of rooms that cease to exist with it
Notes how the difference appears in code: aggregation typically stores a reference or pointer to an object created elsewhere, while composition typically constructs and owns the member directly

text: Why is Java not considered a purely object-oriented language?
expectedAnswerPoints: A purely object-oriented language would treat absolutely everything as an object, and Java does not
Primitive types such as int, char, boolean and double are not objects: they have no methods and do not inherit from Object
Static members belong to the class rather than to any object and can be used without ever creating an instance, which departs from the pure model as well
Wrapper classes and autoboxing exist precisely to bridge the gap, allowing a primitive to be used where an object is required, as in collections
The reason is pragmatic rather than accidental: primitives avoid the memory and indirection overhead of object headers, which matters a great deal in large arrays and arithmetic-heavy code

text: Why use getters and setters rather than making fields public?
expectedAnswerPoints: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it and restricts direct access to internal state, normally by declaring fields private
A setter can validate before assigning, so an invalid value such as a negative age can be rejected outright, which a public field can never do
Accessors also preserve invariants across related fields, so an object cannot be left in a combination of states that should be impossible
They give logical independence: the internal representation can change while the accessor signature stays the same, so no calling code needs modifying

Notes the honest caveat that a getter and setter pair that merely exposes a field with no validation adds nothing over a public field, and that immutability, where state is set once in the constructor and never changed afterwards, is often a stronger guarantee than encapsulation through setters
